claim: Serotonin is an evolutionarily ancient molecule that functions in generating and modulating many behavioral states.
source: Serotonin is an evolutionarily ancient molecule that functions in generating and modulating many behavioral states.
evidence: This is a general statement about serotonin that draws from established scientific knowledge about its evolutionary conservation and functional roles.

claim: In the nematode C. elegans, serotonin neurons that drive female reproductive behavior are directly modulated by inhibitory neuropeptides.
source: In the nematode C. elegans, serotonin neurons that drive female reproductive behavior are directly modulated by inhibitory neuropeptides.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript and references to prior literature.

claim: The n5209 and n6122 mutations affect the T-type calcium channel CCA-1 and symmetrically re-tune its voltage-dependencies of activation and inactivation towards more hyperpolarized potentials.
source: The corresponding mutations affect the T-type calcium channel CCA-1 and symmetrically re-tune its voltage-dependencies of activation and inactivation towards more hyperpolarized potentials.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from Xenopus oocytes expressing mutant channels (Figure 4).

claim: The shift in voltage dependency of CCA-1 strongly and specifically bypasses the behavioral and cell physiological effects of peptidergic inhibition on serotonin neurons.
source: This shift in voltage dependency strongly and specifically bypasses the behavioral and cell physiological effects of peptidergic inhibition on serotonin neurons.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays (Figure 1) and calcium imaging data (Figure 7).

claim: T-type calcium channels are critical regulators of a C. elegans serotonergic circuit.
source: Our results indicate that T-type calcium channels are critical regulators of a C. elegans serotonergic circuit and demonstrate a mechanism in which T-type channels functionally gate inhibitory modulation in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic, behavioral, and physiological data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: T-type channels functionally gate inhibitory modulation in vivo.
source: Our results indicate that T-type calcium channels are critical regulators of a C. elegans serotonergic circuit and demonstrate a mechanism in which T-type channels functionally gate inhibitory modulation in vivo.
evidence: This mechanism is demonstrated through the suppression of peptidergic inhibition by re-tuned T-type channels.

claim: In the vertebrate central nervous system, serotonin is released by a small population of neurons that project widely and exert influence on neural circuits throughout the brain.
source: In the vertebrate central nervous system, the neuromodulator serotonin is released by a small population of neurons that project widely and exert influence on neural circuits throughout the brain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate serotonergic systems.

claim: Serotonin is required for central control of basic physiological functions such as thermoregulation and respiratory control.
source: Serotonin is required for central control of basic physiological functions such as thermoregulation and respiratory control (Myers, 1981; Morin et al., 1990; Frazer and Hensler, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Serotonergic systems control aggression.
source: For example, serotonergic systems control aggression (Kravitz, 1988), appetite (Lent, 1985; Hatcher et al., 2008; Oh et al., 2015), and sexual behavior (Uphouse, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kravitz, 1988.

claim: Serotonergic systems control appetite.
source: For example, serotonergic systems control aggression (Kravitz, 1988), appetite (Lent, 1985; Hatcher et al., 2008; Oh et al., 2015), and sexual behavior (Uphouse, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lent, 1985; Hatcher et al., 2008; Oh et al., 2015.

claim: Serotonergic systems control sexual behavior.
source: For example, serotonergic systems control aggression (Kravitz, 1988), appetite (Lent, 1985; Hatcher et al., 2008; Oh et al., 2015), and sexual behavior (Uphouse, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uphouse, 2014.

claim: Dysregulation of endogenous serotonin systems is thought to underlie psychiatric illness, notably affective disorders such as major depression and generalized anxiety.
source: Dysregulation of endogenous serotonin systems is thought to underlie psychiatric illness, notably affective disorders such as major depression and generalized anxiety (Holmes et al., 2003; Neumeister et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holmes et al., 2003; Neumeister et al., 2004.

claim: Female reproductive behavior (egg laying) in C. elegans requires serotonin, which is released from a pair of Hermaphrodite-Specific Neurons (HSNs).
source: Female reproductive behavior - egg laying - requires serotonin, which is released from a pair of Hermaphrodite-Specific Neurons (HSNs) (Trent et al., 1983; Desai and Horvitz, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Trent et al., 1983; Desai and Horvitz, 1989.

claim: The egg-laying circuit comprises three cell-types: the serotonergic HSNs, the cholinergic ventral cord neurons VC4 and VC5, and electrically coupled vulval and uterine muscles.
source: The egg-laying circuit comprises three cell-types: the serotonergic HSNs, the cholinergic ventral cord neurons VC4 and VC5, and electrically coupled vulval and uterine muscles, of which the vulval muscles (VMs) receive direct synaptic input from motor neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the circuit diagram in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: HSNs synapse both onto VM muscle targets and onto VC4 and VC5 motor neurons.
source: HSNs synapse both onto VM muscle targets and onto VC4 and VC5 motor neurons.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data from White et al., 1986.

claim: VC4 and VC5 motor neurons synapse onto VMs.
source: VC4 and VC5 motor neurons synapse onto VMs (White et al., 1986) and also provide extrasynaptic inhibitory modulation to the HSNs (Bany et al., 2003; Shyn et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 1986.

claim: VC4 and VC5 motor neurons provide extrasynaptic inhibitory modulation to the HSNs.
source: VC4 and VC5 motor neurons synapse onto VMs (White et al., 1986) and also provide extrasynaptic inhibitory modulation to the HSNs (Bany et al., 2003; Shyn et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bany et al., 2003; Shyn et al., 2003.

claim: The G protein-coupled neuropeptide receptor EGL-6 is expressed by HSNs and mediates their inhibition in response to FLP-10 and FLP-17 neuropeptides.
source: The G protein-coupled neuropeptide receptor EGL-6 is expressed by HSNs and mediates their inhibition in response to FLP-10 and FLP-17 neuropeptides.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript (Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008; Kim and Li, 2004).

claim: FLP-10 inhibitory neuropeptides are secreted from several neuron types, as well as from epithelial cells of the reproductive system.
source: FLP-10 inhibitory neuropeptides are secreted from several neuron types, as well as from epithelial cells of the reproductive system.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: FLP-17 peptides are secreted by a small number of cells and are principally released by a pair of chemosensory neurons, the BAGs.
source: FLP-17 peptides are secreted by a small number of cells and are principally released by a pair of chemosensory neurons, the BAGs (Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008; Kim and Li, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008; Kim and Li, 2004.

claim: Both inhibitory cholinergic and peptidergic modulation of the HSNs are mediated by the Go alpha ortholog GOA-1.
source: Both inhibitory cholinergic and peptidergic modulation of the HSNs are mediated by the Go alpha ortholog GOA-1, which acts through two effectors to mediate neuronal inhibition: the diacylglycerol kinase DGK-1 and inward rectifying potassium channels comprising IRK-1 subunits (Nurrish et al., 1999; Emtage et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nurrish et al., 1999; Emtage et al., 2012.

claim: GOA-1 acts through two effectors to mediate neuronal inhibition: the diacylglycerol kinase DGK-1 and inward rectifying potassium channels comprising IRK-1 subunits.
source: Both inhibitory cholinergic and peptidergic modulation of the HSNs are mediated by the Go alpha ortholog GOA-1, which acts through two effectors to mediate neuronal inhibition: the diacylglycerol kinase DGK-1 and inward rectifying potassium channels comprising IRK-1 subunits (Nurrish et al., 1999; Emtage et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nurrish et al., 1999; Emtage et al., 2012.

claim: A point mutation in the neuropeptide receptor EGL-6 causes it to transduce excess inhibitory signaling and thereby inactivates the HSNs.
source: A point mutation in the neuropeptide receptor EGL-6 causes it to transduce excess inhibitory signaling and thereby inactivates the HSNs.
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008) and behavioral data in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of HSNs by EGL-6(gf) receptors requires its endogenous ligands.
source: Inhibition of HSNs by this mutant receptor requires its endogenous ligands (Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008), indicating that EGL-6(gf) receptors are not constitutively active but rather amplify peptidergic inhibition received by HSNs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008.

claim: EGL-6(gf) receptors are not constitutively active but rather amplify peptidergic inhibition received by HSNs.
source: Inhibition of HSNs by this mutant receptor requires its endogenous ligands (Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008), indicating that EGL-6(gf) receptors are not constitutively active but rather amplify peptidergic inhibition received by HSNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for endogenous ligands.

claim: The n5209 suppressor mutation strongly and specifically suppresses the effects of excess peptidergic inhibition onto serotonin neurons.
source: Here, we report that cca-1, which encodes a voltage-gated calcium channel homologous to vertebrate T-type calcium channels, mutates to strongly and specifically suppress the effects of excess peptidergic inhibition onto serotonin neurons.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing suppression of egl-6(gf) phenotype (Figure 1).

claim: egl-6(gf) mutants bloat with unlaid eggs.
source: As a consequence of increased inhibition onto the HSNs, egl-6(gf) mutants bloat with unlaid eggs.
evidence: This is supported by visual observation (Figure 1A) and behavioral assays.

claim: egl-6(gf) n5209 mutants are not bloated with unlaid eggs.
source: egl-6(gf) mutants that also carry the n5209 suppressor mutation are not bloated with unlaid eggs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by visual observation in Figure 1A.

claim: egl-6(gf) mutants released late-stage embryos.
source: Consistent with their having reduced rates of egg laying, egl-6(gf) mutants released late-stage embryos.
evidence: This is supported by the egg-stage distribution data in Figure 1B.

claim: egl-6(gf) n5209 mutants released earlier stage embryos that had not yet undergone extensive morphogenesis, similar to wild type animals.
source: By contrast, egl-6(gf) n5209 mutants released earlier stage embryos that had not yet undergone extensive morphogenesis, similar to wild type animals (Figure 1B; P-values for all noted comparisons are in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the egg-stage distribution data in Figure 1B.

claim: n5209 strongly suppressed the egl-6(gf) phenotype but had little effect on the egg-laying defects of egl-47(gf) and egl-10(lf) mutants.
source: We found that n5209 strongly suppressed the egl-6(gf) phenotype but had little effect on the egg-laying defects of egl-47(gf) and egl-10(lf) mutants (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by the egg-stage distribution data in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: The gene affected by n5209, like irk-1, is not generally required for inhibitory Go signaling in HSNs but has a privileged function with respect to signaling downstream of receptors for inhibitory neuropeptides.
source: These data suggest that the gene affected by n5209, like irk-1, is not generally required for inhibitory Go signaling in HSNs but has a privileged function with respect to signaling downstream of receptors for inhibitory neuropeptides.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of suppression for egl-6(gf) but not egl-47(gf) or egl-10(lf).

claim: n5209 alone had no measurable effect on the developmental stage of newly laid eggs.
source: We observed that n5209 alone had no measurable effect on the developmental stage of newly laid eggs (Figure 1B, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by the egg-stage distribution data in Figure 1B.

claim: n5209 does not grossly affect the timing of egg-laying behavior.
source: These data suggest that n5209 does not grossly affect the timing of egg-laying behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect on egg stage distribution.

claim: The behavior of n5209 mutants, like that of the wild type, switched between active and inactive states and displayed a very similar temporal structure.
source: We observed that the behavior of n5209 mutants, like that of the wild type, switched between active and inactive states and displayed a very similar temporal structure (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the raster plots in Figure 1E.

claim: One parameter of the model used to describe the behavior is altered in n5209 mutants: the time constant that defines the rate with which the egg-laying system 'resets' after a behavioral event.
source: We noted that one parameter of the model used to describe the behavior is altered in n5209 mutants: the time constant that defines the rate with which the egg-laying system 'resets' after a behavioral event (Figure 1F and G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: n5209 mutants display slightly longer intervals between egg-laying events when the system is in an active state.
source: As a result, n5209 mutants display slightly longer intervals between egg-laying events when the system is in an active state.
evidence: This is inferred from the altered time constant.

claim: The overall structure of the reproductive behavioral program is intact in n5209 mutants.
source: However, the overall structure of the reproductive behavioral program is intact in n5209 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral analysis showing similar temporal structure.

claim: The n5209 mutation restores behavior to egl-6(gf) mutants and does not simply cause unregulated activation of the reproductive neuromusculature.
source: These data indicate that the n5209 mutation restores behavior to egl-6(gf) mutants and does not simply cause unregulated activation of the reproductive neuromusculature.
evidence: This is inferred from the intact behavioral structure in n5209 mutants.

claim: The n5209 and n6122 suppressor mutations affect the T-type calcium channel gene cca-1.
source: Because we mapped the n5209 mutation to a small interval that contains only one mutation that affects protein-coding sequence and because the identical mutation was recovered independently by our screen, we concluded that the n5209 and n6122 suppressor mutations affect the T-type calcium channel gene cca-1.
evidence: This is supported by genetic mapping, sequencing, and independent recovery of the same mutation.

claim: cca-1 encodes the pore-forming subunit of a low-voltage activated (LVA) T-type calcium channel and is the only T-type calcium channel gene encoded by the C. elegans genome.
source: cca-1 encodes the pore-forming subunit of a low-voltage activated (LVA) T-type calcium channel and is the only T-type calcium channel gene encoded by the C. elegans genome (Shtonda and Avery, 2005; Steger et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shtonda and Avery, 2005; Steger et al., 2005.

claim: n5209 and n6122 are predicted to affect a proline residue in a short cytoplasmic loop that connects the voltage-sensing domain (transmembrane domain 4) to transmembrane domain 5.
source: n5209 and n6122 are predicted to affect a proline residue in a short cytoplasmic loop that connects the voltage-sensing domain (transmembrane domain 4) to transmembrane domain 5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the protein structure diagram in Figure 2B.

claim: The linker connecting the voltage-sensing domain to transmembrane domain 5 is highly conserved among T-type calcium channels from diverse animal phyla.
source: This linker is highly conserved among T-type calcium channels from diverse animal phyla (Senatore et al., 2014) and the proline affected by the n5209 and n6122 suppressor mutation is invariant between vertebrates and nematodes, suggesting its functional importance (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Senatore et al., 2014 and sequence alignment in Figure 2C.

claim: The proline affected by the n5209 and n6122 suppressor mutation is invariant between vertebrates and nematodes, suggesting its functional importance.
source: This linker is highly conserved among T-type calcium channels from diverse animal phyla (Senatore et al., 2014) and the proline affected by the n5209 and n6122 suppressor mutation is invariant between vertebrates and nematodes, suggesting its functional importance (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment in Figure 2C and inference about functional importance from conservation.

claim: cca-1(n5209) is a semi-dominant suppressor of the egl-6(gf) phenotype.
source: We noted that cca-1(n5209) is a semi-dominant suppressor of the egl-6(gf) phenotype (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3A showing partial suppression in heterozygotes.

claim: A deletion allele of cca-1 - ad1650 - did not suppress egl-6(gf) as well as did cca-1(n5209).
source: Also, a deletion allele of cca-1 - ad1650 - did not suppress egl-6(gf) as well as did cca-1(n5209) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3B.

claim: cca-1(ad1650) caused an egg-laying defect.
source: Furthermore, cca-1(ad1650) caused an egg-laying defect (Figure 3C), whereas cca-1(n5209) mutants exhibited wild-type egg-laying behavior (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3C.

claim: cca-1(n5209) mutants exhibited wild-type egg-laying behavior.
source: Furthermore, cca-1(ad1650) caused an egg-laying defect (Figure 3C), whereas cca-1(n5209) mutants exhibited wild-type egg-laying behavior (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1B.

claim: n5209 does not simply cause loss of cca-1 function but rather alters the function of the CCA-1 T-type calcium channel to restore behavior to egl-6(gf) mutants.
source: These data indicate that n5209 does not simply cause loss of cca-1 function but rather alters the function of the CCA-1 T-type calcium channel to restore behavior to egl-6(gf) mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of n5209 and deletion allele effects.

claim: The P262S suppressor mutation shifted the current-voltage relationship of T-type channels towards more hyperpolarized potentials.
source: We observed that the P262S suppressor mutation shifted the current-voltage relationship of T-type channels towards more hyperpolarized potentials (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the I-V curves in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The suppressor mutation shifted both the steady-state activation and inactivation curves.
source: The suppressor mutation shifted both the steady-state activation and inactivation curves.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figures 4C and 4F.

claim: The peak conductance was shifted by −10 mV, with wild-type channels exhibiting peak conductance at −20 mV and mutant channels exhibiting peak conductance at −30 mV.
source: The peak conductance was shifted by −10 mV, with wild-type channels exhibiting peak conductance at −20 mV and mutant channels exhibiting peak conductance at −30 mV (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 4C.

claim: The half-activation potential was shifted by −7 mV, from −37.14 ± 2.4 mV (wild-type) to −44.69 ± 1.4 mV (mutant).
source: The half-activation potential was shifted by −7 mV, from −37.14 ± 2.4 mV (wild-type) to −44.69 ± 1.4 mV (mutant).
evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological measurements reported in the text and Figure 4H.

claim: The half-inactivation potential shifted from −58.18 ± 0.7 mV (wild-type) to −63.11 ± 0.3 mV (mutant).
source: The half-inactivation potential shifted from −58.18 ± 0.7 mV (wild-type) to −63.11 ± 0.3 mV (mutant) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 4F.

claim: The slope factor (k) was unchanged for both steady-state activation and inactivation.
source: The slope factor (k) was unchanged for both steady-state activation and inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by the values reported in Figure 4H.

claim: Mutant channels pass a window current over a range of more hyperpolarized potentials than do wild-type channels, but the width of that range is not significantly affected.
source: These data indicate that mutant channels pass a window current over a range of more hyperpolarized potentials than do wild-type channels, but the width of that range is not significantly affected (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by the window current analysis in Figure 4G.

claim: The cca-1 suppressor mutation enhanced the suppression by loss of goa-1 function.
source: We found that the cca-1 suppressor mutation enhanced the suppression by loss of goa-1 function (Figure 5A), suggesting that the cca-1 suppressor mutation has an effect in parallel to G proteins in the control of cellular inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5A.

claim: The cca-1 suppressor mutation has an effect in parallel to G proteins in the control of cellular inhibition.
source: We found that the cca-1 suppressor mutation enhanced the suppression by loss of goa-1 function (Figure 5A), suggesting that the cca-1 suppressor mutation has an effect in parallel to G proteins in the control of cellular inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhancement of suppression.

claim: cca-1(n5209) enhanced the suppression of the egl-6(gf) phenotype by mutation of the ligand-encoding genes flp-10 and flp-17.
source: We also found that cca-1(n5209) enhanced the suppression of the egl-6(gf) phenotype by mutation of the ligand-encoding genes flp-10 and flp-17 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5B.

claim: cca-1(n5209) had no measurable effect on animals that lack HSNs.
source: However, cca-1(n5209) had no measurable effect on animals that lack HSNs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5C.

claim: Although CCA-1 acts in parallel to EGL-6, it nevertheless depends on the HSNs to modify reproductive behavior.
source: These data indicate that although CCA-1 acts in parallel to EGL-6, it nevertheless depends on the HSNs to modify reproductive behavior (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect in HSN-ablated animals.

claim: Both the cholinergic VC4 and VC5 neurons and the serotonergic HSNs strongly expressed cca-1::GFP.
source: Both the cholinergic VC4 and VC5 neurons and the serotonergic HSNs strongly expressed cca-1::GFP (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the expression pattern shown in Figure 6B.

claim: cca-1::GFP is expressed in many neurons in the head, tail, and in the ventral cord.
source: We also observed cca-1::GFP expression in many neurons in the head (Figure 6A), tail (data not shown), and in the ventral cord.
evidence: This is supported by the expression pattern shown in Figure 6A.

claim: cca-1::GFP is expressed in the non-neuronal distal tip cells of the somatic gonad.
source: We also observed cca-1::GFP expression in the non-neuronal distal tip cells of the somatic gonad (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the expression pattern shown in Figure 6B.

claim: LIN-39 was required for cca-1 expression in VC4 and VC5 neurons.
source: We found that LIN-39 was required for cca-1 expression in VC4 and VC5 neurons (Figure 6C and D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data in lin-39 mutants shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: cca-1 expression in HSNs was not affected by lin-39 mutation.
source: By contrast, cca-1 expression in HSNs was not affected by lin-39 mutation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data in lin-39 mutants shown in Figure 6C.

claim: lin-39 mutation did not strongly modify the suppression of egl-6(gf) by cca-1(n5209), strongly suggesting that cca-1 expression in VC4 and VC5 is dispensable for its function as a suppressor of peptidergic inhibition.
source: We next tested whether lin-39 was required for the ability of cca-1(n5209) to suppress egl-6(gf). lin-39 mutation did not strongly modify the suppression of egl-6(gf) by cca-1(n5209), strongly suggesting that cca-1 expression in VC4 and VC5 is dispensable for its function as a suppressor of peptidergic inhibition (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: HSN expression of cca-1 dsRNA potently reverted the suppression conferred by cca-1(n5209).
source: HSN expression of cca-1 dsRNA potently reverted the suppression conferred by cca-1(n5209) (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi data in Figure 6G.

claim: When cca-1(RNAi) was expressed in vulval muscles and in VC4 and VC5, no significant effect on the suppression of the egl-6(gf) phenotype by CCA-1(n5209) channels was observed.
source: When we expressed cca-1(RNAi) in vulval muscles and in VC4 and VC5, we did not observe any significant effect on the suppression of the egl-6(gf) phenotype by CCA-1(n5209) channels (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi data in Figures 6H and 6I.

claim: CCA-1(n5209) mutant T-type channels act in the HSNs themselves.
source: Together, these data indicate that CCA-1(n5209) mutant T-type channels act in the HSNs themselves.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific RNAi experiments.

claim: Re-tuning T-type channels renders the cells in which they are expressed insensitive to peptidergic inhibition.
source: Thus, re-tuning T-type channels renders the cells in which they are expressed insensitive to peptidergic inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the HSN-specific function of the mutant channels.

claim: Wild-type HSNs displayed spontaneous calcium transients.
source: Wild-type HSNs displayed spontaneous calcium transients (Figure 7A and C, top), consistent with previous reports (Shyn et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 7A and C and citations to prior work.

claim: HSNs of egl-6(gf) mutants were largely silent, and only rarely did a calcium transient occur in these mutant HSNs.
source: By contrast, HSNs of egl-6(gf) mutants were largely silent, and only rarely did we observe a calcium transient in these mutant HSNs (Figure 7A and C, second panel).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 7A and C.

claim: The cca-1(n5209) suppressor mutation restored activity to egl-6(gf) HSNs.
source: Strikingly, the cca-1(n5209) suppressor mutation restored activity to egl-6(gf) HSNs (Figure 7A–D), but the calcium transients in egl-6(gf) cca-1(n5209) mutant HSNs were lower in amplitude and occurred at a higher frequency than those of wild-type HSNs.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figures 7A-D.

claim: The calcium transients in egl-6(gf) cca-1(n5209) mutant HSNs were lower in amplitude and occurred at a higher frequency than those of wild-type HSNs.
source: Strikingly, the cca-1(n5209) suppressor mutation restored activity to egl-6(gf) HSNs (Figure 7A–D), but the calcium transients in egl-6(gf) cca-1(n5209) mutant HSNs were lower in amplitude and occurred at a higher frequency than those of wild-type HSNs.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figures 7A-D.

claim: Similar low-amplitude, high-frequency calcium transients were observed in the HSNs of cca-1(n5209) single mutants.
source: We observed similar low-amplitude, high-frequency calcium transients in the HSNs of cca-1(n5209) single mutants (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 7A and C.

claim: In HSN somas of egl-6(gf) cca-1(n5209) mutants, cumulative △F/F was significantly elevated compared to that measured in the somas of egl-6(gf) HSNs but was still lower than cumulative ∆F/F measured in the somas of wild-type HSNs.
source: In HSN somas of egl-6(gf) cca-1(n5209) mutants, cumulative △F/F was significantly elevated compared to that measured in the somas of egl-6(gf) HSNs but was still lower than cumulative ∆F/F measured in the somas of wild-type HSNs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the cumulative calcium data in Figure 7B.

claim: In HSN axons, cumulative △F/F of the egl-6(gf) cca-1(n5209) neurons was strikingly similar to that measured in wild-type axons.
source: In HSN axons, however, cumulative △F/F of the egl-6(gf) cca-1(n5209) neurons was strikingly similar to that measured in wild-type axons.
evidence: This is supported by the cumulative calcium data in Figure 7D.

claim: The complete restoration of cumulative activity in the HSN neurite correlated with the complete restoration of reproductive behavior conferred to egl-6(gf) mutants by the cca-1(n5209) mutation.
source: This complete restoration of cumulative activity in the HSN neurite correlated with the complete restoration of reproductive behavior conferred to egl-6(gf) mutants by the cca-1(n5209) mutation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a correlation observed between the physiological and behavioral data.

claim: cca-1(n5209) restores activity to HSNs that have been silenced by excess peptidergic inhibition.
source: These data show that cca-1(n5209) restores activity to HSNs that have been silenced by excess peptidergic inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data.

claim: T-type channels regulate axonal, that is, presynaptic, calcium in serotonergic HSNs.
source: These data further suggest that T-type channels regulate axonal, that is, presynaptic, calcium in serotonergic HSNs and that altering the voltage-gating of T-type channels may have a larger effect on axonal/presynaptic calcium than it does on calcium signaling in the HSN cell body.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on soma vs. neurite calcium.

claim: Altering the voltage-gating of T-type channels may have a larger effect on axonal/presynaptic calcium than it does on calcium signaling in the HSN cell body.
source: These data further suggest that T-type channels regulate axonal, that is, presynaptic, calcium in serotonergic HSNs and that altering the voltage-gating of T-type channels may have a larger effect on axonal/presynaptic calcium than it does on calcium signaling in the HSN cell body.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on soma vs. neurite calcium.

claim: The window current might play a critical role in setting the resting potential of serotonergic HSNs.
source: The window current might play a critical role in setting the resting potential of serotonergic HSNs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on known properties of T-type channels.

claim: Inhibitory neuropeptides require GIRK-like potassium channels to inhibit HSNs, and it is therefore likely that inhibitory neuropeptides hyperpolarize HSNs.
source: We previously showed that inhibitory neuropeptides require GIRK-like potassium channels to inhibit HSNs, and it is therefore likely that inhibitory neuropeptides hyperpolarize HSNs (Emtage et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from prior work on GIRK channels.

claim: Re-tuned T-type channels might be active at hyperpolarized potentials and thereby pass a depolarizing current that brings the membrane potential of HSNs back to their pre-modulator baseline.
source: Re-tuned T-type channels might be active at these hyperpolarized potentials and thereby pass a depolarizing current that brings the membrane potential of HSNs back to their pre-modulator baseline.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the suppression.

claim: In the absence of inhibitory peptides, the resting potential of HSNs would be such that re-tuned T-type channels are inactivated.
source: Importantly, in the absence of inhibitory peptides, the resting potential of HSNs would be such that re-tuned T-type channels are inactivated.
evidence: This is inferred from the voltage-dependence of the mutant channels.

claim: Re-tuned T-type channels could have little effect on circuit function in the absence of hyperpolarizing modulatory inputs, which is consistent with the observation that re-tuned T-type channels have little effect on C. elegans reproductive behavior in the absence of peptidergic inhibition.
source: Re-tuned T-type channels could have little effect on circuit function in the absence of hyperpolarizing modulatory inputs, which is consistent with our observation that re-tuned T-type channels have little effect on C. elegans reproductive behavior in the absence of peptidergic inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data and the proposed mechanism.

claim: Re-tuned T-type channels might boost small depolarizing inputs onto HSNs that are hyperpolarized by peptidergic inhibition and allow those depolarizing inputs to drive behavior.
source: Re-tuned T-type channels might boost small depolarizing inputs onto HSNs that are hyperpolarized by peptidergic inhibition and allow those depolarizing inputs to drive behavior.
evidence: This is a proposed alternative mechanism.

claim: T-type channels can boost depolarizations generated by cell-intrinsic mechanisms, for example in cardiac myocytes and their C. elegans counterparts, pharyngeal muscle cells.
source: T-type channels can also boost depolarizations generated by cell-intrinsic mechanisms, for example in cardiac myocytes (Hagiwara et al., 1988; Zhou and Lipsius, 1994; Mangoni et al., 2006) and their C. elegans counterparts, pharyngeal muscle cells (Shtonda and Avery, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Re-tuned T-type channels restored wild-type behavior to animals in which HSNs receive excess inhibition, but the pattern of HSN activity in these animals was strikingly different from that in the wild type.
source: Re-tuned T-type channels restored wild-type behavior to animals in which HSNs receive excess inhibition, but the pattern of HSN activity in these animals was strikingly different from that in the wild type.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data showing different patterns of activity.

claim: In the wild type, low-frequency, high-amplitude calcium transients were observed in HSN cell bodies and neurites.
source: In the wild type, we observed low-frequency, high-amplitude calcium transients in HSN cell bodies and neurites.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 7.

claim: Under the conditions used to record HSN activity, calcium transients did not correlate with egg laying or muscle contractions.
source: Under the conditions we used to record HSN activity these calcium transients did not correlate with egg laying or muscle contractions (data not shown), and only rarely did we observe egg laying by immobilized animals.
evidence: This is based on observations during calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Collins et al. recorded HSN activity in freely moving animals and showed that HSNs are active during periods of behavioral quiescence.
source: Recently, Collins et al. recorded HSN activity in freely moving animals and showed that HSNs are active during periods of behavioral quiescence (Collins et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2016.

claim: The data are inconsistent with a model in which the HSNs function as typical motor neurons to acutely drive target muscle contractions.
source: Notably, our data and those of Collins et al. are inconsistent with a model in which the HSNs function as typical motor neurons to acutely drive target muscle contractions.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between HSN activity and muscle contractions.

claim: Peptidergic inhibition through the neuropeptide receptor EGL-6 strongly affected calcium transients in HSNs; almost none of the egl-6(gf) mutant HSNs displayed any calcium transients.
source: Peptidergic inhibition through the neuropeptide receptor EGL-6 strongly affected calcium transients in HSNs; almost none of the egl-6(gf) mutant HSNs displayed any calcium transients.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 7.

claim: The cca-1 suppressor mutation strikingly reduced the amplitude and increased the frequency of HSN calcium transients.
source: On its own, the cca-1 suppressor mutation strikingly reduced the amplitude and increased the frequency of HSN calcium transients.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data in Figure 7.

claim: High-frequency, low-amplitude transients in cca-1 mutant HSNs were not affected by increased peptidergic inhibition.
source: These high-frequency, low-amplitude transients in cca-1 mutant HSNs were not affected by increased peptidergic inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data comparing cca-1(n5209) and egl-6(gf) cca-1(n5209).

claim: HSNs carrying re-tuned T-type channels were functionally disengaged from inhibitory peptidergic modulation at the level of cell physiology as well as behavior.
source: That is, HSNs carrying re-tuned T-type channels were functionally disengaged from inhibitory peptidergic modulation at the level of cell physiology as well as behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging and behavioral data.

claim: The cumulative activity of cca-1 mutant HSNs was comparable to that of wild-type HSNs.
source: Although the calcium transients of wild-type and cca-1 mutant HSNs were clearly different, we found that the cumulative activity of cca-1 mutant HSNs was comparable to that of wild-type HSNs.
evidence: This is supported by the cumulative calcium data in Figure 7.

claim: Reproductive behavior is not driven by fast, phasic signaling from HSNs.
source: These data suggest that reproductive behavior is not driven by fast, phasic signaling from HSNs, as might be suggested by the direct innervation of vulval muscles by serotonergic HSNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different patterns of activity produce similar behavior.

claim: HSN targets integrate signals from HSNs over longer periods.
source: Instead, our data indicate that HSN targets integrate signals from HSNs over longer periods.
evidence: This is inferred from the cumulative activity analysis.

claim: Bursts of reproductive behavior are separated by twenty to thirty minutes of quiescence.
source: On average, bursts of reproductive behavior are separated by twenty to thirty minutes of quiescence, suggesting that the timescale over which such an integrative mechanism would function is on the order of tens of minutes.
evidence: This is based on the behavioral analysis.

claim: The timescale over which an integrative mechanism would function is on the order of tens of minutes.
source: On average, bursts of reproductive behavior are separated by twenty to thirty minutes of quiescence, suggesting that the timescale over which such an integrative mechanism would function is on the order of tens of minutes.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral timing.

claim: Vertebrates possess three genes that encode T-type channels, each of which is expressed in many central circuits.
source: Unlike C. elegans, whose genome encodes only one T-type channel, vertebrates possess three genes that encode T-type channels, each of which is expressed in many central circuits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate T-type channels.

claim: The duplication of T-type calcium genes in vertebrate phyla could reflect expanded and diversified roles for T-type channels that are analogous to their function in the C. elegans serotonin system.
source: The duplication of T-type calcium genes in vertebrate phyla could reflect expanded and diversified roles for T-type channels that are analogous to their function in the C. elegans serotonin system.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in C. elegans.

claim: Different T-type channel isoforms might be involved in the gating of multiple modulatory systems in the vertebrate brain.
source: If so, different T-type channel isoforms might be involved in the gating of multiple modulatory systems in the vertebrate brain.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in C. elegans.

claim: Alleles of T-type channel genes are strongly linked to heritable epilepsy.
source: Alleles of T-type channel genes are strongly linked to heritable epilepsy (Kim et al., 2001; Heron et al., 2004; Khosravani et al., 2005; Singh et al., 2007; Powell et al., 2009) and neuropathic pain (Bourinet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Alleles of T-type channel genes are linked to neuropathic pain.
source: Alleles of T-type channel genes are strongly linked to heritable epilepsy (Kim et al., 2001; Heron et al., 2004; Khosravani et al., 2005; Singh et al., 2007; Powell et al., 2009) and neuropathic pain (Bourinet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bourinet et al., 2016.

claim: A T-type channel variant is associated with autism spectrum disorders.
source: A T-type channel variant is also associated with autism spectrum disorders (Splawski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Splawski et al., 2006.

claim: T-type channels are required in thalamic circuits for normal sleep, in midbrain centers for central processing of nociception, and in cerebellar circuits for motor learning.
source: T-type channels are required in thalamic circuits for normal sleep, in midbrain centers for central processing of nociception, and in cerebellar circuits for motor learning (Anderson et al., 2005; Park et al., 2010; Ly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2005; Park et al., 2010; Ly et al., 2013.

claim: In brain regions where T-type channels function, altering T-type channels might affect receptivity of neural circuits to modulatory inputs.
source: Our study raises the intriguing possibility that in these brain regions altering T-type channels might affect receptivity of neural circuits to modulatory inputs and that defective gating of neuromodulation might be an underlying cause of pathologies associated with T-type channel dysfunction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in C. elegans.

claim: Defective gating of neuromodulation might be an underlying cause of pathologies associated with T-type channel dysfunction.
source: Our study raises the intriguing possibility that in these brain regions altering T-type channels might affect receptivity of neural circuits to modulatory inputs and that defective gating of neuromodulation might be an underlying cause of pathologies associated with T-type channel dysfunction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in C. elegans.

claim: T-type channel isoforms are differentially regulated by diverse intracellular signaling systems, including systems that couple to protein kinases C and A and heterotrimeric G proteins.
source: T-type channel isoforms are differentially regulated by diverse intracellular signaling systems, including systems that couple to protein kinases C and A and heterotrimeric G proteins (Wolfe et al., 2003; Park et al., 2003, 2006; Kim et al., 2006; DePuy et al., 2006; Hu et al., 2009; Perez-Reyes, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: T-type channel genes encode transcripts that display a high degree of alternative splicing to generate multiple channel isoforms from a single locus.
source: Furthermore, T-type channel genes encode transcripts that display a high degree of alternative splicing to generate multiple channel isoforms from a single locus (Senatore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Senatore et al., 2014.

claim: Neurons can remodel the complement of T-type channels either through genetic programs and mechanisms that couple neural activity to mRNA splicing, or acutely regulate T-type channels through canonical second messenger signaling pathways and effectors.
source: Neurons can, therefore, remodel the complement of T-type channels either through genetic programs and mechanisms that couple neural activity to mRNA splicing, or acutely regulate T-type channels through canonical second messenger signaling pathways and effectors (Murbartián et al., 2004; Senatore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Murbartián et al., 2004; Senatore et al., 2014.

claim: A gating function of T-type channels with respect to neuromodulation would be subject to a high degree of selective control and possess a large capacity for plasticity.
source: Because of this regulation, in the vertebrate brain a gating function of T-type channels with respect to neuromodulation would be subject to a high degree of selective control and possess a large capacity for plasticity.
evidence: This is inferred from the regulatory mechanisms described.

claim: T-type calcium channels could be important therapeutic targets for psychiatric disorders linked to defects in neuromodulatory systems.
source: The hypothesis that T-type channels gate neuromodulatory inputs to circuits implies that T-type calcium channels could be important therapeutic targets for psychiatric disorders linked to defects in neuromodulatory systems.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in C. elegans.

claim: Compounds that alter the voltage-dependencies of T-type channels might synergize with therapeutics that directly target monoamine signaling in the brain.
source: Based on our studies of a model serotonergic circuit in C. elegans, we suggest that compounds that alter the voltage-dependencies of T-type channels might synergize with therapeutics that directly target monoamine signaling in the brain.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in C. elegans.

claim: Globally manipulating T-type channel function in the brain could affect specific circuits.
source: Furthermore, our studies demonstrate the possibility that globally manipulating T-type channel function in the brain could affect specific circuits.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity observed in C. elegans.

claim: T-type channels are widely expressed in the C. elegans nervous system, as they are in the vertebrate brain.
source: T-type channels are widely expressed in the C. elegans nervous system, as they are in the vertebrate brain, but in C. elegans, re-tuning T-type channels by mutation had a striking effect on the modulation of a circuit that controls reproductive behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the expression data in Figure 6 and knowledge about vertebrate expression.

claim: In C. elegans, re-tuning T-type channels by mutation had a striking effect on the modulation of a circuit that controls reproductive behavior.
source: T-type channels are widely expressed in the C. elegans nervous system, as they are in the vertebrate brain, but in C. elegans, re-tuning T-type channels by mutation had a striking effect on the modulation of a circuit that controls reproductive behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral and physiological data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The origins of the apparent specificity of T-type channel effects are in the combination of the biophysical basis of inhibition of serotonin neurons and the manner in which serotonin signals are processed by a downstream circuit.
source: Our data suggest that the origins of this apparent specificity are in the combination of in the biophysical basis of inhibition of serotonin neurons and the manner in which serotonin signals are processed by a downstream circuit.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on voltage-dependence and signal integration.

claim: Similar cellular and circuit mechanisms likely exist in the vertebrate brain.
source: It is highly likely that similar cellular and circuit mechanisms exist in the vertebrate brain, and when the pharmacological tools become available it will be important to test whether manipulating vertebrate T-type channels restores function to neural circuits in and behavior of animal models of psychiatric disorders associated with monoamine dysfunction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in C. elegans.
